comments: Under anaerobic conditions, the multifunctional enzyme AdhE catalyzes the sequential reduction of acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde and then to ethanol (see the mixed acid fermentation pathway). The two catalytic functions are conferred by its N-terminal aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) domain and C-terminal iron-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) domain. The unusual quarternaty structure of AdhE was noticed very early; 20-60 subunits are helically arranged to form rod-like ultrastructures that appear to change conformation in the presence of Fe 2+ and NADH [ Kessler92 ]. More recently, cryo-EM structures confirmed the higher-order helical architecture and conformational changes upon cofactor addition [ Kim19 , Pony20 , Kim20 ]. The two active sites are topologically separated; ALDH active sites face the outer surface, while ADH active sites face the inner surface [ Kim19 ]. Helical filament formation is essential for AdhE function in vitro and in vivo ; the extended conformation allows substrate channeling between the two active sites [ Pony20 , Kim20 ]. Crystal structures of the apo- and cofactor-bound alcohol dehydrogenase domain of AdhE have been solved at 1.95 and 1.65 Å resolution, respectively [ Azmi20 ]. Using a method that distinguishes N-phosphorylation from O-phosphorylation, N-phosphorylation was detected in vitro [ Hu20 ]. AdhE is one of the major proteins damaged by oxidative stress, and its expression is low under aerobic conditions [ Tamarit98 ]. However, AdhE mutants that confer the ability to grow aerobically on ethanol can be selected [ MembrilloHernan00 ]; their in vivo activity depends on protection against metal-catalyzed oxidation by the chaperone DnaK [ Echave02 ]. A Glu568Lys substitution identified in the adhC mutant also confers high activity of the enzyme under aerobic assay conditions [ HollandStaley00 ]. AdhE's aerobic role is uncertain, but it may protect against oxidative stress, acting as a hydrogen peroxide scavenger [ Echave03 ]. Under aerobic conditions, AdhE may be protected against metal-catalyzed oxidation in the presence of copper [ Matuszewska08 ] and heat inactivation [ Matuszewska09 ] by the heat shock proteins IbpA and IbpB. AdhE appears to interact directly with the ribosome at the head of the small subunit, where it may unwind RNA helices [ Shasmal16 ]. Ribosomes containing the rrsH variant of the 16S rRNA have enhanced interactions with AdhE, leading to phenotypic changes [ Kurylo18 ]. In the pathogenic E. coli O157:H7, AdhE activity affects the regulation of virulence genes in various ways; an adhE mutant is significantly less virulent than wild type [ Beckham14 ]. The pyruvate formate-lyase deactivase activity of AdhE described by [ Kessler91 , Kessler92 ] has been questioned. [ Nnyepi07 ] were unable to reproduce the PFL deactivase activity; they noted that small molecule thiols can effect deactivation. Expression of adhE is induced under anaerobic [ Kessler91 , Chen91 , Leonardo93 , Aristarkhov96 ] and microaerobic [ Peng03 ] growth conditions and repressed in the presence of nitrate [ Chen91 ]. The half-maximal increase (pO 0.5 ) for adhE expression is at 0.8 mbar oxygen [ Becker97 ]. adhE expression is correlated with the NADH:NAD + ratio in the cell [ Leonardo93 , Leonardo96 ]. Transcriptional regulation is complex; expression involves two promoter regions, is repressed by Cra [ Mikulskis97 ] and NarL in the presence of nitrate [ MembrilloHernan99a ], and induced by Fis [ MembrilloHernan99 , MembrilloHernan99a ] and FNR [ MembrilloHernan99a ]. RNase III cleavage of the adhE mRNA is required for translation, perhaps eliminating a secondary structure that occludes the ribosome binding site [ Aristarkhov96 ]. adhE mRNA is a target for degradation by RNase G [ Umitsuki01 , Kaga02 , Jourdan08 , Ito13 ]. Mutants overproducing alcohol dehydrogenase are able to use ethanol as the sole source of carbon [ Clark80 ]. Temperature-sensitive mutants have been isolated [ Lorowitz82 , Cunningham86a ]. Null mutants are unable to grow anaerobically with glucose unless an external electron acceptor such as nitrate is supplied [ Casse76 , Pascal81 , Kessler91 ]. An F670E mutant disrupts the helical superstructure and affects ALDH catalytic activity more significantly in the direction of acetyl-CoA reduction [ Kim19 ]. A Δ446-449 mutant that shortens the linker between the ALDH and ADH domains also prevents helical filament formation and affects ALDH catalytic activity, and phenocopies a Δ adhE mutant in vivo [ Pony20 ]. In the metabolic engineering field, deletion of adhE is a determinant in the production of compounds such as succinate [ Singh11 ], D-lactate [ Zhou11 ], and polyhydroxyalkanoates [ Jian10 ]. ana : [ Casse76 ] adhC : " a lcohol d e h ydrogenase c onstitutive mutant" [ Clark80 ] AdhE: " a lcohol d e h ydrogenase e nzyme" [ Lorowitz82 ] Reviews: [ Clark89 , Sawers04a , Sawers04 ]

Catechol 2,3-dioxygenase is an extradiol type dioxygenase that catalyzes the conversion of catechol to (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate with the insertion of two atoms of molecular oxygen. The enzyme from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 has been purified to homogeneity [ Nakai83 ]. The enzyme, which is a homotetramer, contains 1 atom of iron per monomer. Activity ranges betweent 110 to 300 μmol/min/mg protein, depending on iron concentration. The enzyme is very sensitive to oxygen [ Nakai83 ]. The xylE gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned and sequenced [ Nakai83a ].

The xylH gene, found on the pWW0 plasmid of Pseudomonas putida mt-2 , encodes a tautomerase that is involved in the meta cleavage pathway of catechol degradation. The enzyme catalyzes the tautomerization among different forms of 4-oxalocrotonate [ Whitman91 , Whitman92 , Chen92a ]. Initially the authors suggested that the enzyme catalyzes the isomerization of the keto form 4-oxalocrotonate to the keto form (3 E )-2-oxohex-3-enedioate via the dienol form (2 Z ,4 E )-2-hydroxyhexa-2,4-dienedioate . However, it is now known that the enzyme catalyzes only the conversion of the two latter forms, and that 4-oxalocrotonate is formed non-enzymatically. The enzyme is a complex of extremely small subunits, of only 62 amino acids [ Chen92a ]. While the initial report found that the enzyme had a pentameric structure [ Chen92a ], later work, performed with a related enzyme isolated from Pseudomonas sp. CF600 , indicated that the complex is in fact a hexamer with 32 symmetry [ Roper94 , Subramanya96 ]. The enzyme from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 was crystalized, and its structure determined to 2.4 Å resolution, showing that the enzyme complex is a trimer of dimers, where each dimer consists of a four-stranded beta-sheet with two antiparallel alpha-helices on one side [ Taylor98a ]. The enzyme is highly efficient, with Kcat/K M values approaching the diffusion-controlled limit [ Whitman91 ]. The xylH gene has been cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli , and the recombinant protein was produced in yields of at least 10 mg of pure enzyme/liter of culture and purified [ Chen92a ].

2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 forms a complex with 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase that converts (3 E )-2-oxohex-3-enedioate to ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate via the intermediate (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate (although it was previously suggested that the intermediate is (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate [ Harayama89 , Stanley00 ]). The protein is very unstable on its own, and the only successful attempt to overexpress it was conducted by coexpressing the two enzymes simultaneously [ Stanley00 ].

2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase and 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 form a complex that converts 4-oxaloisocrotonate to ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate . Recent work suggests that the product of 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase and the substrate of 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase is the unstable compound (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate , a tautomer of 2-oxopent-4-enoate . Since this compound is very unstable, it is possible that the reason for the formation of this complex is to provide an efficient transfer of the intermediate between the two enzymes [ Harayama89 , Stanley00 ].

2-Hydroxymuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase from Pseudomonas putida mt-2 was initially mis-characterized as benzaldehyde dehydrogenase [ Shaw90 ]. Later work identifed the true nature of this enzyme, which is encoded by the xylG gene [ Inoue95 ]. The enzyme is active towards the ring-cleavage products of catechol and 4-methylcatechol ( (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate and (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-5-methyl-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate , respectively), but not the ring cleavage product of 3-methylcatechol ( (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate ) [ Inoue95 ]. The enzyme accepts benzaldehyde as a product, but with much reduced activity.

The final two steps of the meta -cleavage pathway in Pseudomonas sp. CF600 involve the conversion of ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate to pyruvate and acetyl-CoA by the enzymes 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) . Biochemical studies demonstrated that these two enzymes comprise a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase heterodimer, and suggest that the product of the aldolase reaction, acetaldehyde , is transferred to the dehydrogenase active site via a channeling mechanism. This minimizes the risk to the cells posed by the toxic acetaldehyde . The heterodimer has been crystallized and its structure determined. The assymetric unit contains four DmpFG heterodimers [ Manjasetty01 ].

The subunit stoichiometry of this complex has not been reported. These two enzymes from Bordetella sp. 10d appear to form a high molecular weight complex with an apparent molecular mass of 470 kDa as determined by gel filtration chromatography. The two enzymes co-purified and resolved to bands of 29 kDa and 27 kDa on SDS-PAGE. The molar ratio of the two enzymes in the complex was 1:1 [ Orii06 ]. Similar complexes between these two enzymes have been found in other species (see 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (AmnE) and 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (XylI)). The amino-terminal amino acid sequences of the 29 kDa and 27 kDa bands were distinct and analysis identified them as the decarboxylase and hydratase, respectively [ Orii06 ].

2-hydroxypentadienoate hydratase (MhpD) converts 2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate (HPD) into 4-hydroxy-2-ketopentanoate [ Pollard98a , Ferrandez97 ]. E. coli is able to utilize certain aromatic acids as carbon and energy sources. A meta-cleavage pathway involving MhpD is used for the catabolism of 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)propionate [ Burlingame83 ].

The final two steps of the meta -cleavage pathway in Pseudomonas sp. CF600 involve the conversion of ( S )-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate to pyruvate and acetyl-CoA by the enzymes 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) . Biochemical studies demonstrated that these two enzymes comprise a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase heterodimer, and suggest that the product of the aldolase reaction, acetaldehyde , is transferred to the dehydrogenase active site via a channeling mechanism. This minimizes the risk to the cells posed by the toxic acetaldehyde . The reaction is stimulated by Mn 2+ and by NADH , and, to a lesser extent, NAD + [ Powlowski93 ].

The subunit structure of this enzyme has not been reported. This enzyme from Bordetella sp. 10d catalyzes the decarboxylation of (3 E )-2-oxohex-3-enedioate to form the common aromatic degradation intermediate (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate and CO 2 . This decarboxylase appears to form a high molecular weight complex with 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase . The complex apparent molecular mass was 470 kDa as determined by gel filtration chromatography. The two enzymes co-purified and resolved to bands of 29 kDa and 27 kDa on SDS-PAGE. The molar ratio of the two enzymes in the complex was 1:1 [ Orii06 ]. Similar complexes formed by these two enzymes have been found in other species (see 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (AmnE) and 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase (XylI)). The amino-terminal amino acid sequences of the 29 kDa and 27 kDa bands were distinct and analysis identified them as the decarboxylase and hydratase, respectively [ Orii06 ]. The gene encoding this enzyme in Bordetella sp. 10d has not been characterized. See the compound page for 4-oxaloisocrotonate for 4-oxalocrotonate nomenclature clarification.
